What Did We Develop?
The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive 3D web application that turns decades of NASA Earth observations into procedural music and real-time telemetry. Built with Three.js and the Web Audio API, it runs friction-free in any browser without external plugins.

How Did It Address the Challenge?
NASA challenged participants to make Earth science multi-sensory through sound. We solved this by mapping open satellite datasets—NASA GISTEMP temperatures, NSIDC Arctic ice loss, OCO-2

Why Is It Important?
Traditional climate data is purely visual, excluding blind and visually impaired individuals. Our platform bridges this divide through data sonification, high-contrast modes, and spoken narration. Hearing Earth’s vital signs evolve from calm bass tones into discordant warnings transforms abstract numbers into an immediate, emotional experience—empowering science classrooms, museums, and the global public to truly listen to our changing planet.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox

Our project, Earth Information Jukebox, transforms complex NASA Earth observation data into an interactive musical experience. When you explore climate data through static charts or dense spreadsheets, it can feel abstract and distant. We wanted to change that by turning satellite data into sound. Using the browser’s native Web Audio API and Three.js, our web app maps real multi-decade NASA measurements directly into musical notes, tempo, and timbre. As you scrub through history, an interactive 3D globe rotates in space, its atmospheric halo shifting dynamically while procedural melodies play—calm, deep tones for balanced climate eras, climbing into urgent, higher octaves as global temperatures spike.

We designed the Jukebox around four core NASA datasets: GISTEMP surface temperature anomalies, NSIDC Arctic sea ice extent, OCO-2 atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and FIRMS wildfire detections. We chose to constrain the sonification to musical pentatonic scales so the data produces an emotional, cinematic soundscape rather than harsh, chaotic noise. The 3D planet responds in real time to the music with audio-reactive shockwaves and a live frequency spectrum visualizer.

The greatest benefit of our project is universal accessibility. Traditional satellite imagery and climate graphs are completely visual, leaving out blind and visually impaired people. By pairing data sonification with live voice telemetry and high-contrast modes, we created a platform where anyone can experience planetary science. For educators and museums, it provides a zero-installation tool that makes students lean in and truly listen to what our planet is experiencing.

We built the entire application using lightweight web standards—HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, Three.js for WebGL rendering, and Web Audio API for sound synthesis. A major factor our team prioritized was keeping the platform completely client-side and lightweight, ensuring it runs smoothly on any basic laptop or mobile phone anywhere in the world without requiring powerful GPUs or external downloads. Ultimately, we hope the Earth Information Jukebox bridges the gap between scientific data and human emotion, turning space observation into an unforgettable sensory journey.
